title: Who gets to call the water “safe” – Spilling the Truth Workshop (7 October 2026)
content:
by Jakleen Al-Dalal’a

For someone checking a storm overflow map before a swim, the question may seem straightforward: is it safe to enter the water? In our online workshop, participants questioned what a “safe” label would mean for people swimming, paddling or working beside a river. Their discussion raised a further question about the advice a map might offer: what would readers need to know before deciding whether it applied to their own activity and circumstances?

title: What a Storm Overflow Alert Leaves Unsaid – Spilling The Truth Workshops (14 and 24 September 2026)
content:
by Jakleen Al-Dalal’a

When an overflow map reports that a discharge has stopped, what does that tell someone standing beside the water?

The map may no longer show an active release. It cannot necessarily tell them what was discharged, how much entered the river, where it has travelled, or whether other sources of pollution are present. Yet people may consult that same map before swimming, taking children paddling, or bringing a group of volunteers to the river.

title: Five communities around Lobeke National Park set up and mapping!
content:
Since the last post we’ve conducted two fieldwork trips to Lobeke National Park. Fair to say it’s pretty out of the way – three days by 4X4 on mud roads ridden with muddy ravines in the rainy season and clouds of dust in the dry. But for this reason the area is pretty special, monkeys playing and peering down at you even in villages and around the base camp, gorillas commonly spotted along the tracks of forest, elephants meandering around as they please.

The abundance of animals and tight controls on community activities through the conservation service has however certainly created problems – local communities and particularly the Indigenous Baka hunter-gatherers have great fear of entering the forest due to rangers on patrol and so do not have access to the quantity and diversity of forest produce they rely on. That the farmed food that they are now increasingly encouraged to produce is regularly ravaged by monkeys, gorillas, porcupines and elephants leaves them trapped with little ability to get the nutrition they need.

title: Spilling the Truth: Rethinking River Lea’s Storm Overflow Crisis Maps
content:
by Jakleen Al-Dalal’a and Artemis Skarlatidou

When a combined sewer overflow releases sewage into a river, how do people actually find out, and do they trust what they are being told? 

On 18 July 2026, residents, river users, and representatives from local organisations and community groups met at UCL East to work through that question together. The session is part of CHRYSES Project, a European research collaboration examining how environmental health crises are understood, remembered and communicated. It forms part of a growing series of workshops and events exploring these questions across different rivers and communities and following on from an earlier session in which participants mapped what crisis along the River Lea actually looks and feels like, drawing on memory, routine and everyday use of the river rather than official and formal data. Across both sessions, a consistent concern has been how lived experience and public data meet – or fail to meet – when people try to understand what is happening to the rivers they care about.

title: Report on the 2nd Citizen Science Africa Conference
content:
I recently attended the 2nd Citizen Science Africa Conference, held on 2 – 3 July 2026 at the University of Lagos, Nigeria. The conference theme Citizen Science, Technologies and Artificial Intelligence for Africa’s Transformation, provided a strong platform for examining how citizen science can contribute to environmental and urban decision-making across African contexts, particularly where operational realities demand robust methods, credible validation, and responsible data governance.

The conference keynote address strengthened this theme, a marvelous presentation by Prof. Tolullah Oni (Clinical Professor, University of Cambridge; Founder/CEO, UrbanBetter) on “Urban Better Cityzens, Health Data, and Technological Infrastructure in Africa” who beautifully connected data infrastructure and technological systems to real-world transformation agendas. Prof. Peter Elias (Professor of Geography, University of Lagos; Co-Chair, CtiSci Africa Association) made a presentation on “UNSD Collaborative on Citizen Data and its Implementation: Beyond Data to Transformative Policies in Africa”.

title: Rethinking Crisis through the Humanities – Reflections from Paris
content: This week we had the opportunity to attend the “Living with Permacrisis: Care, Responsibility, Agency and Art” conference organised by the UCD Humanities institute (https://www.ucd.ie/humanities/) and hosted by the Centre Universitaire de Norvège à Paris – Fondation Maison des sciences de l’homme ( https://www.fmsh.fr/). Bringing together scholars from philosophy, literature, history, cultural studies, art, geography and the environmental humanities, this two-day conference explored a timely question; what does it actually mean to live with crisis when crisis no longer feels exceptional, but increasingly becomes the background condition of everyday life?

title: Stories from the River Lea: community voices shaping understanding of environmental change
content:
Environmental crises are often monitored through technical indicators, datasets, and institutional reporting. Yet they are also lived, sensed, and negotiated through everyday experience, in how people notice change, remember loss, and care for the environments around them. What happens when these lived experiences become a form of evidence? How can mapping capture crises not only as a physical condition but as a social and embodied reality? 

On 31 January 2026, residents, river users, and local community organisations came together at UCL East for a participatory workshop exploring lived experiences of crisis along the River Lea. The session formed part of the CHRYSES project [https://chryses.aalto.fi/], an international research collaboration that examines how environmental health crises are understood, remembered, and communicated through maps, stories, and community knowledge. The workshop was delivered in collaboration with Manifold: a new art project for UCL Multi Lab that creates opportunities for multi-directional learning between UCL and its local communities.

title: Participatory mapping, led by students and experts from across Central Africa
content:
by Simon Hoyte

The ambition of Extreme Citizen Science and our mapping tool Sapelli has always been to co-develop projects with Indigenous Peoples, local communities, and locally based organisations which reach a point where we, as implementers from London, become redundant.

Often in the projects I have co-designed in Cameroon alongside hunter-gatherers, despite this intention of making myself redundant, there remains certain aspects which depend on my input and problem solving. These are most often the technical aspects such as if the communities want to change their Sapelli projects, the Sapelli app goes heywire, or the phone starts to misbehave. As much as I try to include time during my fieldtrips to train local facilitators in how to tackle all of these potential problems, I can never cover everything and up until now much of the Sapelli system was complicated to manage.

title: IN.FOR.BIO – our new 6-year One Health project
content:
By Simon Hoyte & Jerome Lewis

The world is waking up to the deep connection between human, animal, plant, and environmental health. 

The concept of ‘One Health’, coined by the vet William Karesh in 2003, is now a hot topic, rising high on international agendas after the COVID-19 pandemic. One Health simply refers to how ‘the health of humans, domestic and wild animals, plants, and the wider environment (including ecosystems) are closely linked and interdependent’ (WHO). 

‘By linking humans, animals and the environment, One Health can help to address the full spectrum of disease control – from prevention to detection, preparedness, response and management – and contribute to global health security’. 

But One Health is much more than disease control, it concerns the wellbeing of environments and all their inhabitants. It is about plant and animal health, food and water security, cultural and spiritual ties to animals, plants, and the environment, addressing human rights violations and much more.

title: Indigenous floor maps and many names for ice: ICA Vancouver 2025
content:
by Timothie Biggs

Here are a few highlights from the 32nd International Cartographic Association (ICA) 2025 Conference in Vancouver, British Colombia, Canada.


Firstly, the highlight of the map gallery was a walkable floor map – the ‘Indigenous Atlas’ created by Canada Geographic – it’s been around for some time so perhaps you have already encountered it – if not here is more on the McMaster University website or Canadian Geographic.

This was one of a number of maps/presentations related to Canada’s indigenous people that were spotlighted throughout the conference. Another interesting one was a project in Canada’s northern regions to surface the many names for ice used by elders to help build maps for navigation warning amongst increasingly unpredictable ice melt along water-based transit routes.
